title: Add a runtime library linked into native and JIT code
description: Code generation currently calls printf, fflush, exit and malloc directly. Add a runtime (Rust or C, built with the compiler) that both the linked executable and the JIT import: allocation, string printing and concatenation, polymorphic equality, raising built-in exceptions, and reporting an uncaught exception with SML/NJ's message and exit status. Linking must keep working with `cc` (NASSAU_CC) and in the JIT without a system linker.
acceptance_criteria: Compiled programs and the REPL call the same runtime entry points; allocation goes through it.
close_reason: Completed by c170d4f (Build a typed middle end for code generation, #13); the shared runtime was subsequently refactored to Rust in bf16994.

title: Choose a uniform runtime value representation
description: Polymorphic functions, datatypes and closures need values of one machine size. Decide and document: which values are immediate (int, char, bool, unit, nullary constructors) and which are pointers to heap blocks (tuples, records, constructors with arguments, closures, refs, strings, boxed reals, exception packets); the heap block header layout (size and tag) that a later GC can walk; and the width and overflow behaviour of int. SML/NJ uses a 31-bit int here (Int.maxInt = 1073741823) and MLton a 32-bit one; Nassau currently uses i32 like MLton.
acceptance_criteria: A design note in the repo describes the representation and the int width decision, and the current list representation is migrated to it.
close_reason: Completed by c170d4f (Build a typed middle end for code generation, #13); the shared runtime was subsequently refactored to Rust in bf16994.

title: Lower typed programs to a core IR before Cranelift
description: Add a small intermediate language between the typed AST and Cranelift: named values in A-normal form, explicit closures (closure conversion with free-variable lists), explicit allocation, and decision trees for matches. Code generation then only translates the IR. The IR should be dumpable (--dump-ir already exists for Cranelift IR; add e.g. --dump-core) so fixtures can assert on it.
acceptance_criteria: The features the backend supports today go through the new IR, with a dump flag for it.
close_reason: Completed by c170d4f (Build a typed middle end for code generation, #13); the shared runtime was subsequently refactored to Rust in bf16994.

title: Build a typed middle end for code generation
description: Today codegen.rs walks the AST directly and gets types from the old monomorphic checker in sema.rs, which only knows int, real, string, bool, unit and lists. The backend needs the types HM inference already computes, a value representation that works for polymorphic code, and an intermediate form where closures and pattern matching are explicit.
acceptance_criteria: Code generation reads types from infer.rs, lowers through a core IR, and the existing compiled and REPL fixtures still pass.
close_reason: Completed by c170d4f (Build a typed middle end for code generation, #13); the shared runtime was subsequently refactored to Rust in bf16994.

Keep the resolved type of each expression and pattern (after defaulting overloads and freezing weak variables) in a side table keyed by node, and expose it to code generation. Overloaded operators (+, <, ...) must record the type they resolved to.
acceptance_criteria: A debug flag or dump shows the resolved type of every node; overloaded operators carry their resolved type.

title: Compile the full SML core to native code
description:
Slices nassau-ugc.2 to .10 parse and type-check the SML'97 core and module language, but the Cranelift backend and the JIT REPL still only compile simple `val` bindings, arithmetic, comparisons, `if`, lists and `print`. Everything else type-checks and is then rejected as "not supported yet". This epic makes the backend compile everything the front end accepts, for both native executables and the REPL, with runtime fixtures checked against SML/NJ.

Order: the typed middle end (value representation, core IR, runtime library) comes first, then functions and closures, since almost everything else depends on them. Tuples, pattern matching, datatypes, exceptions, references and modules build on those. REPL parity, garbage collection and fixture coverage run alongside.
acceptance_criteria: Every program the front end accepts either compiles and runs with the same output and exit status as SML/NJ, or is rejected with a documented reason. The REPL handles the same programs.

acceptance_criteria: Core SML’97 language constructs are implemented in staged, reviewable slices with fixture coverage; remaining gaps are explicit before Basis Library work begins.

title: Conformance import infrastructure: vendoring, provenance, triage
description: Shared plumbing for the suite imports. Decide the layout (proposal: tests/fixtures/conformance/<suite>/ plus <suite>.unsupported/ and error/ subtrees). Each vendored file records its upstream repo, path and commit in a header comment; each suite directory carries the upstream licence (Poly/ML LGPL-2.1, SML/NJ BSD-3, MLton's own licence, HaMLet doc/LICENSE.txt). Nassau itself has no licence yet, so confirm vendoring is acceptable. Write a Python import tool that fetches a pinned commit, runs each program through Poly/ML and Nassau, and sorts it: passes -> fixture; Poly/ML accepts and Nassau fails -> *.unsupported; must-reject -> error/; needs Basis Nassau lacks -> excluded with a nassau-617 reference; implementation extension or harness-specific (use, PolyML.*, SMLofNJ, MLton.*) -> excluded with reason. The exclusion list is checked in so re-imports are reproducible. Needs a policy for programs whose output is nondeterministic or implementation-specific (timings, addresses, exnName formats).
design:
Layout per suite $name (hamlet, mlton, smlnj):
- tests/fixtures/$name/ : passing fixtures, plus upstream LICENSE and PROVENANCE (repo, commit, import date, local edits).
- tests/fixtures/$name.unsupported/ : Poly/ML accepts, Nassau fails. Existing harness prints the git mv once one passes.
- tests/fixtures/$name.ignored/ : Poly/ML itself cannot pass the program (it differs from MLton/SML/NJ/HaMLet). First line is a comment saying so and why. The harness must not run these dirs.
The only oracle is Poly/ML; no Definition-based or .ok-file expectations. Poly/ML Tests/ is excluded (LGPL-2.1).
Import tool sorts: Poly/ML+Nassau pass -> $name; Poly/ML passes, Nassau fails -> $name.unsupported; Poly/ML fails -> $name.ignored; must-reject -> error/; Basis gap -> nassau-617 list.
acceptance_criteria: Tool and layout documented in docs/development.md; re-running the tool on a pinned commit is idempotent.

title: Implement compact Rust interpreter for core IR
description: Add a portable Rust execution backend for Nassau core IR so the same language frontend can run client side in WebAssembly. Aim for approximately 500 lines of interpreter implementation where practical, without dropping existing language semantics. Keep the Cranelift backend available for native execution.
design: Interpret the existing closure-converted block IR after parsing, inference and lowering. Prefer compact explicit execution frames and browser-compatible heap storage over native code pointers or dependencies on the native MMTk runtime. The approximately 500-line target is a design goal, not permission to omit semantics or obscure the implementation.
acceptance_criteria: Supports every current Atom, Prim, Op, Stmt and Term variant, including recursive closures, globals, references, structural equality, integer overflow and exceptions. Tail calls do not grow the Rust stack. Value storage has a defined reclamation strategy for persistent sessions and cyclic references. Validate using fixtures in tests/fixtures or tests/repl; add no unit tests.
notes: Implemented a 475-line core-IR interpreter in src/interpreter.rs using boa_gc 0.22.0 and derived tracing; no custom collector or unsafe backend code. gc 0.5.1 was tested but overflowed its recursive tracer on existing 100k/200k list fixtures, so the user approved Boa. Added a reusable library API, explicit execution frames, proper tail calls and exception propagation, precise closure-held global dependencies, retain_globals, captured byte output, and file-only --interpret CLI. Validation: full cargo test --locked --workspace passed (755 fixture trials, 12 documented interpreter skips, native REPL and MMTk object-model fixture); 203 interpreter fixture trials passed. Final targeted exception/runtime/byte-output checks and strengthened standalone session fixture passed. Clippy with -D warnings, formatting and diff checks passed. Isolated build of src/lib.rs with only boa_gc compiled for wasm32-unknown-unknown and wasm32-wasip1; the actual session/cycle-reclamation fixture ran successfully as wasm32-wasip1 under Node WASI. title: Verify bounded-memory GC behavior in native and REPL fixtures
description: Establish the parent feature's acceptance with allocation-heavy programs that retain little live data, in both execution modes. Add regression fixtures and developer documentation for the supported collector.
design: Use tests/fixtures and tests/repl only, with PolyML oracle checks for SML semantics. Make reclamation assertions deterministic through a fixed small heap or runtime heap counters rather than flaky RSS thresholds. Run substantially more total allocations than the heap limit; include a retaining-live-data control. Cover dead/live cycles, escaped closures, exception allocation, mutable refs, static literals, recursive stack roots and repeated REPL rebinding. Distinguish managed-heap bounds from any separately retained JIT code. Document the pinned MMTk version/plan, root model, heap/stress settings and deferred moving/generational features.
acceptance_criteria: An allocation-heavy native loop and repeated REPL phrases run within the configured managed-heap bound while allocating far more than that bound. Fixtures fail if collection is disabled or roots are omitted. Full fixture/REPL suites, relevant PolyML oracle checks, formatting and clippy pass. The parent is closed only after real collection meets these gates.

title: Enable MMTk MarkSweep collection and mutator coordination
description: Enable actual reclamation using MMTk's non-moving MarkSweep plan once object tracing and all root sources are implemented. Replace NoGC as the normal collecting configuration.
design: Implement Collection and ActivePlan lifecycle, collector worker startup, stop/resume/block mutator coordination and allocation slow paths. A single SML mutator still requires synchronization with MMTk worker threads. Start collection only after runtime and root registries are ready. Expose a bounded heap configuration and a deterministic GC stress option for fixtures; specify allocation-failure behavior. Keep weak references/finalization explicitly unsupported until Nassau has those features. Do not enable moving or generational plans without their required pointer updates/barriers. Plan reference: https://www.mmtk.io/status.
acceptance_criteria: Both native executables and the REPL complete multiple forced MarkSweep cycles with a small configured heap. Live graphs survive, unreachable graphs are reclaimed, worker coordination does not deadlock, and exhaustion has a defined tested outcome. No collection runs against uninitialized runtime state or unpublished objects. Existing fixtures retain observable behavior.
notes: Production MarkSweep is already implemented as the default, with fixed 32 MiB heap, one worker, NoGC opt-in, configurable heap and allocation-interval stress, initialized object publication, and single-mutator Condvar coordination. Validated native million-iteration unreachable cyclic allocation and REPL shadowing under 8 MiB heaps, every-allocation root fixtures, full workspace under periodic forced collection, object-model cyclic reclamation, optimized/unoptimized native/JIT execution, and defined exhaustion diagnostic/status 1. All checks pass; unsupported moving/generational/weak/finalization features remain excluded.
close_reason: Completed collecting runtime integration, functor root pruning, and production native/JIT stress validation

title: Expose generated stack roots and runtime temporary roots to MMTk
description: Make every live managed value visible at a collection safepoint in both native and JIT code. Cranelift currently represents Nassau values as I64 and does not identify roots automatically.
design: Identify managed/tagged values through lowering and use the pinned Cranelift frontend stack-map APIs. Emit/register maps and implement a reliable frame walk for both modes; validate ABI, frame-pointer/unwind requirements and optimized tail calls before choosing the mechanism. Register JIT maps before executing a chunk and retain them for executable-code lifetime; include equivalent metadata in native artifacts. If stack-map walking proves unsuitable, document and implement an explicit precise shadow-stack fallback. Register runtime/host temporary roots across nested allocations, printing and exception construction, including partially built objects and derived/interior pointers. Define generated-to-runtime transitions and safepoint publication for MMTk worker scanning.
acceptance_criteria: Native and REPL fixtures force collection while the only references reside in locals, arguments, closure captures, recursive frames or runtime temporaries. Cover optimized/unoptimized code, nested exception allocation and string helpers. Frames/maps remain valid across calls and returning/unwinding paths; no live pointer depends on conservative register discovery.
notes: Completed production validation after global root integration: full workspace passes with NASSAU_GC_STRESS=1000 and 32 MiB heap (552 fixtures, REPL, object model). Native/JIT mmtk-frames and mmtk-safepoints additionally pass at every-allocation collection under 8 MiB with opt-level none and speed-and-size. Nested locals, arguments, mutual closures, recursive frames, exceptions and helper temporaries survive collection; Clippy passes.
close_reason: Completed collecting runtime integration, functor root pruning, and production native/JIT stress validation

title: Manage global and persistent REPL roots without retaining dead history
description: Register generated globals and runtime roots, then define persistent REPL root lifetimes so shadowed, inaccessible values can be collected while values reachable from old closures remain valid.
design: Root runtime exception identities, raised/uncaught state, current top-level bindings and host-visible SML values. Register native and JIT global cells before they can contain heap pointers. Old closures can load earlier global cells directly, so simply removing roots for shadowed names is unsafe; rooting every historical chunk forever also defeats REPL bounded memory. Track reachable chunk/global dependencies or change global environments so reachability is represented in the managed graph. JIT machine-code unloading is outside the initial scope, but old code must keep its maps and required roots while callable. Clarify root updates when phrases fail or raise.
acceptance_criteria: REPL fixtures repeatedly shadow large values and demonstrate reclamation of inaccessible heap history. Closures saved before rebinding still access their original values after collection. Cross-phrase exceptions, refs, type descriptors and printer-held values survive forced GC. Native global values survive GC and root registrations have defined lifetimes.
notes: Completed functor root pruning: each visible functor retains declaration-time bindings named by its body, referenced structures, exception patterns/replications, and transitive applied-functor dependencies rather than the entire lexical environment. Compiler environments remain available for elaboration. New mmtk-functor-history fixture retains forty functors alongside repeatedly shadowed 262144-byte strings under an 8 MiB heap with every-allocation collection, while preserving original structure/exception dependencies through a forwarding functor. Full stress workspace and optimized/unoptimized JIT checks pass. Syntactic analysis conservatively retains matching outer names shadowed in a body and all exports of referenced structures; documented.
close_reason: Completed collecting runtime integration, functor root pruning, and production native/JIT stress validation

title: Package the shared MMTk runtime and allocation lifecycle
description: Replace the direct-rustc runtime build with dependency-aware packaging that includes MMTk in the archive embedded for generated native artifacts and in the runtime used by the JIT. Route all generated allocation sites through the binding.
design: Preserve NASSAU_CC linking and the existing runtime ABI where practical. Initialize one MMTk instance per process and bind the SML mutator once; repeated REPL chunks share it. Implement checked physical byte sizing, alignment, allocation semantics and post_alloc. Define the contract for header/payload initialization and prevent tracing partially initialized objects; the root task covers nested allocation temporaries. Cover dynamic string allocations as well as fixed fields. Audit std/no_std, panic strategy and required native link libraries; propagate build failures cleanly.
acceptance_criteria: Native and REPL fixtures run through the shared MMTk allocator under NoGC. Clean builds embed all needed runtime dependencies without duplicate runtime instances or symbols. Zero-field objects, strings including padding/terminator, records, closures, refs and reals allocate with valid sizes/alignment. Existing fixture and REPL suites pass.
notes: Shared Cargo runtime packaging and checked allocation lifecycle implemented. Header and zero payload precede post_alloc; allocation semantics handle large objects and strings include NUL/padding. TLS mutator is reused across REPL chunks and destroyed at thread exit. Native/JIT NoGC and production MarkSweep forced collections pass. Clean runtime build, NASSAU_CC/system-library forwarding and single allocator symbol checks pass. Final workspace validation passed 552 native fixtures, REPL and object-model fixtures, Clippy and formatting.
close_reason: Shared Cargo runtime, checked allocation lifecycle and native/JIT NoGC execution verified by full fixtures, clean build/link smoke and quality gates

title: Implement the Nassau MMTk object model and tagged slots
description: Implement ObjectModel and heap Scanning for Nassau's tagged 64-bit values and existing header format. Use a non-moving MarkSweep-compatible model first.
design: ObjectReference points to the aligned header. Prefer MMTk side metadata where compatible to preserve the current header layout; confirm requirements against the pinned release. Provide physical size calculations. Trace record fields, closure captures excluding the raw code address, and ref contents. Strings and real payloads contain no references. Exception objects and REPL type descriptors use their existing record/ref layouts. A custom Slot must reject odd immediates, zero sentinels and non-managed/static addresses before constructing ObjectReference. Audit static object graphs: trace their managed children explicitly or prove static objects never contain managed references. Implement writable slots without promising moving-plan support yet. Source: https://docs.mmtk.io/api/mmtk/vm/scanning/index.html.
acceptance_criteria: Fixture coverage under forced collection retains shared/cyclic live graphs and reclaims dead cycles. Integers, tags, raw code pointers, real bits and string bytes cannot be mistaken for references. All object kinds have correct physical size and field scanning, including zero-length payloads and static literals. Collecting-plan trait paths contain no placeholder panics.
notes: Implemented the non-moving MarkSweep object model with side metadata, checked physical sizes and tagged writable slots. Heap scanning traces records, refs and closure captures while excluding code pointers, real bits, string bytes and static addresses. Executable object-model fixture verifies live/dead membership across two collections, shared/cyclic graphs, large and empty objects. Native and REPL forced-collection fixtures pass at all three optimization levels. Final workspace run passed 552 native fixtures plus REPL and object-model fixtures; Clippy, formatting, clean runtime build, NASSAU_CC/system-library forwarding and single allocator symbol checks passed. Production MarkSweep and generated/global/host roots provide the requested end-to-end evidence.
close_reason: Shared runtime and tagged object model completed end to end; native/REPL forced collections, object-model reclamation, full fixture suites, clean linking and quality gates passed.

title: Prove an MMTk NoGC binding in native and JIT execution
description: Build a minimal Nassau binding against a pinned MMTk release. Prove that the same runtime can allocate through MMTk in a generated native executable and in the REPL. This is an integration spike, not completion of garbage collection.
design: Follow https://docs.mmtk.io/portingguide/howto/nogc.html. Inspect the selected release rather than assuming the online development API. Record the exact version/features, Rust/toolchain/platform requirements, VMBinding traits, singleton initialization, static linkage recipe, and MarkSweep metadata requirements. Current build.rs invokes rustc directly on a no_std runtime and cannot resolve Cargo dependencies. Avoid linking two copies of the runtime or resolving duplicate Rust symbols by allowing multiple definitions.
acceptance_criteria: Checked-in fixture smoke tests allocate and print representative heap values in native and REPL modes using NoGC. Cargo.lock pins the dependency. Record the tested build/link approach and remaining binding requirements in the issue or development docs. NoGC must not be reported as satisfying bounded-memory acceptance.
notes: Pinned MMTk 0.33.0, default features disabled, vo_bit enabled (eager_sweeping). Shared Cargo runtime rlib for JIT and dependency-complete staticlib for native executables; no duplicate runtime linkage. Native archive uses panic=abort/std and rustc native-static-libs; NASSAU_CC retained. Tested rustc 1.100.0-nightly on x86_64 Linux. Native/REPL NoGC fixtures and clean target-directory build/link smoke passed, including symbol-count and linker-library checks. docs/development.md records packaging, traits, metadata and remaining collecting requirements. NoGC does not prove bounded memory.
close_reason: Shared Cargo runtime, checked allocation lifecycle and native/JIT NoGC execution verified by full fixtures, clean build/link smoke and quality gates

title: Integrate MMTk garbage collection in native code and the REPL
description: Replace the never-freed bump heap with a Nassau binding to MMTk. Start with a pinned NoGC integration spike to validate runtime packaging and allocation, then implement precise object tracing, generated/runtime/global roots, REPL root lifetimes and non-moving MarkSweep collection in both execution modes.
design: The initial collecting plan is MarkSweep. NoGC is an intermediate bring-up step only. Preserve tagged-value semantics and initially prefer side metadata over changes to Nassau object headers. Cranelift stack maps provide root metadata, not a collector; Nassau must register/walk those maps and root runtime temporaries. The standalone runtime currently uses direct rustc and needs dependency-aware packaging. Persistent REPL roots must preserve old closure dependencies without retaining every inaccessible historic value. Moving/generational plans and JIT code unloading are deferred. Binding guide: https://docs.mmtk.io/portingguide/howto/nogc.html. Children define the implementation order and concrete acceptance gates.
acceptance_criteria: An allocation-heavy loop that keeps little live data runs within a configured managed-heap bound in compiled code and the REPL, despite total allocations greatly exceeding that bound. Real MMTk collection reclaims unreachable graphs, preserves live roots and old REPL closure dependencies, and does not retain inaccessible REPL heap history. Native and REPL fixtures and existing semantic/oracle suites pass; NoGC alone cannot complete this feature.
